theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: A classroom at the Centre needs a new lighting circuit. Describe the steps you would take to plan the whole job, from first request to handover.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would find out exactly what is wanted: read the work order, look at the drawing and specification, and talk to the instructor about the number and type of lights and where the switches go. Then I would visit the classroom to measure, check the route for the cables and see where the circuit will connect at the panel. Next I would break the job into steps in order: mark out, fix conduit and boxes, pull in cables, fit the lights and switches, connect at the panel, then test and inspect. I would estimate the time for each step and make a simple bar chart. I would list the materials and tools and check they are in the store. I would do a risk assessment, including safe isolation at the panel and work at height. I would agree the plan and the time the power is off with the instructor, plan the quality checks and tests, and plan the clean-up and the report at the end.
markingPoints: Finds out the requirements from the work order, drawing, specification and the person asking
Visits and measures the site
Lists the steps in a sensible order with time estimates
Lists materials and tools and checks they are available
Includes the risk assessment, safe isolation, agreement with the supervisor, checks and handover

essays.stem: Explain where you can find the information you need to plan a job, and why each source is useful.
essays.modelAnswer: The work order or job card tells me what job is to be done, where it is and when it must be finished. The drawings show where things go, such as lights, sockets and the panel, and the scale lets me measure lengths. The specification tells me the type and standard of materials and work, such as the cable size or the type of fittings. The customer or supervisor can explain what they really want and answer questions, so I do not guess. The makers' instructions tell me how to fit and use their products safely. The electrical code and the Centre's rules tell me the safety standards the work must meet so it will pass inspection. Earlier job records and the store's stock list help me check what materials are already there. Using all of these together means the plan is complete and correct before work starts.
markingPoints: Work order or job card: what, where and when
Drawings and specification: positions, sizes, materials and standards
Customer or supervisor: what is really wanted, answers questions
Makers' instructions and the code or Centre's rules: safe fitting and standards to meet
Explains why using these sources gives a complete, correct plan

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out a risk assessment for a job, and explain the order in which hazards should be controlled.
essays.modelAnswer: To carry out a risk assessment I would look at each step of the job and at the place where it will be done, and list the hazards, such as live electricity, work at height, dust from drilling, sharp tools and trip hazards. For each hazard I would write who could be harmed, such as the workers, the customer or the public, and how likely and how bad the harm could be. Then I would decide the controls. The best control is to remove the hazard, for example by isolating the supply so there is no live work. Next is to swap to something safer, such as a lighter ladder or a less dusty tool. Then come guards, barriers and other engineering controls, then safe working methods, signs and training. PPE, such as safety glasses, gloves and boots, is the last line of defence. I would write it all down, explain it to the team before work starts and check it again if the job changes.
markingPoints: Looks at each step and lists the hazards
Says who could be harmed and how likely and how bad
Gives the order of controls: remove, substitute, engineering or barriers, safe methods and training, PPE last
Gives a correct example, such as isolating the supply to remove the electrical hazard
Writes it down, explains it to the team and reviews it when things change

essays.stem: Explain how you would estimate the time, the number of people and the materials for a small wiring job.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by breaking the job into its steps, such as marking out, fixing conduit, pulling cables, fitting accessories, connecting and testing. For each step I would estimate how long it takes, using my own experience and asking the supervisor, and add the times together. I would add some extra time for delays, such as late deliveries or waiting for the power to be isolated. If the job has a deadline, I would work out how many people are needed: for example, 12 labour-hours shared by 3 people takes about 4 hours. For materials I would measure the routes on the drawing using the scale, or on site with a tape, and add about 10% for waste and bends. I would count the boxes, sockets, switches, lights and fixings from the drawing. Then I would check the store for what we already have and order the rest in good time.
markingPoints: Breaks the job into steps and estimates each step's time
Adds extra time for delays
Works out the number of people from labour-hours and the deadline
Measures cable runs and adds an allowance for waste
Counts accessories and fixings, checks stock and orders in time

essays.stem: Describe how you would make a bar chart for a three-day wiring job, and how you would use it while the work is done.
essays.modelAnswer: I would list all the tasks down the left side of a page in the order they must be done, for example mark out, fix conduit and boxes, pull in cables, fit accessories, connect at the panel, test and inspect, and clean up. Across the top I would draw the time, split into the three days and into morning and afternoon. For each task I would draw a bar from when it starts to when it should finish, using my time estimates. Tasks that depend on another task start after it finishes, while tasks that do not depend on each other can run side by side if there are enough people. I would mark key points, such as when the power must be off. While the work is done, I would shade each bar as the task is finished. By comparing the shaded bars with today's date I can see if the job is on time or behind, and tell the supervisor early so we can change the plan.
markingPoints: Lists tasks in order down the side
Shows time across the top, split into days or half-days
Draws a bar for each task from start to finish, with dependent tasks after the ones they need
Marks key points such as the power-off time
Uses the chart to track progress and report delays early

essays.stem: Your job includes adding a socket to an existing circuit. Explain how safe isolation should be planned and carried out.
essays.modelAnswer: In the plan I would write the time the power will be off and tell the customer so they can prepare. I would find out from the panel schedule which breaker feeds the circuit, and make sure I have a lock, a tag, a voltage tester and a proving unit. On the day, I would switch off the breaker for the circuit and fit my lock so that nobody can switch it back on. I would fix a tag with my name, the date and the reason, and keep the key. Then I would check my voltage tester on the proving unit or a known live source to make sure it works. I would test at the socket position between live and neutral, live and earth, and neutral and earth to prove the circuit is dead. Then I would check the tester again on the known source. Only then would work start. I would never work live, and I would follow the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Plans the power-off time and tells the customer
Identifies the correct breaker and has a lock, tag, tester and proving unit
Switches off, locks off and tags, and keeps the key
Checks the tester before use, proves dead between all conductors, checks the tester after
States that work is never done live

essays.stem: Explain who you need to talk to while planning and doing a job, and why each of them needs to be told.
essays.modelAnswer: I need to talk to my supervisor or instructor to agree the plan, the timing and any changes, because they are responsible for the job and can see problems I may miss. I talk to the customer, such as a shop owner, to understand what they want, to tell them when the power will be off, and to agree any extra work, so there are no surprises. My team needs to know the plan, their tasks and the hazards, so I would hold a short toolbox talk at the start. Other trades on site, such as plumbers or painters, need to know where I am working so we do not get in each other's way or damage each other's work. The store keeper or supplier needs my materials list in time so that items arrive when needed. At the end I report to my supervisor on what was done, the test results and any problems.
markingPoints: Supervisor: agrees the plan, timing and changes
Customer: requirements, power-off times, agreed changes
Team: tasks and hazards, for example a toolbox talk
Other trades and the store or supplier: avoid clashes, get materials in time
Reports back at the end

essays.stem: Describe how you would keep a job on track, and what you would do when something does not go to plan.
essays.modelAnswer: Each day I would check the work done against the plan and the bar chart, so that I know whether we are on time. I would check that the materials for the next tasks are on site, so that we are not waiting. If something does not go to plan, for example a beam blocks the cable route or a delivery is late, I would stop and think about the problem and its effect on safety, quality and time. I would not make big changes on my own. I would tell my supervisor, explain the problem and suggest a solution, such as a new route or doing other tasks first. Any change would be agreed, written on the plan and, if the customer is affected, explained to them. If the change brings a new hazard, I would update the risk assessment. Finally, I would record the problem and what was done, so that it can be learned from at the review.
markingPoints: Checks progress against the plan or bar chart regularly
Checks materials and resources for the next tasks
Stops and reports problems to the supervisor rather than changing the plan alone
Agrees changes, updates the plan and the risk assessment, tells the customer if affected
Records the problem and its solution for the review

essays.stem: Explain how you would build quality checks into the plan for a wiring job.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by finding the standard the work must meet from the specification, the drawings, the makers' instructions and the electrical code. Then I would decide on check points during the job instead of waiting until the end. After marking out, I would check positions and heights against the drawing. After fixing conduit and boxes, I would check that they are level, secure and the right size. Before closing the boxes, I would check the cable sizes, the conductor colours and that the terminations are tight. At the end I would plan the inspection and the dead tests in the usual order: continuity of protective conductors, insulation resistance and polarity, with any live tests done only afterwards by a competent person as the rules require. I would plan a record sheet for the results. If a check fails, the work is put right before the next step, so faults are not hidden.
markingPoints: Finds the standard from the specification, drawings, makers' instructions and code
Plans check points during the job, not only at the end
Gives examples of stage checks (positions, fixings, terminations)
Plans the final inspection and dead tests in a sensible order, with results recorded
Puts faults right before moving on

essays.stem: Describe what you would do to finish a job, hand it over and review it.
essays.modelAnswer: When the work is complete and tested, I would make sure all covers and fittings are in place and nothing is left unsafe. I would clean the work area, sweep up dust and off-cuts, and sort waste into the right bins for recycling or disposal. I would return tools and equipment to the store, report any that are damaged, and return spare materials. I would mark any changes on the drawing so that it shows the work as it was really installed. I would fill in the job sheet with the work done, the materials used, the test results and the time taken. At handover I would show the customer what was done, where the breaker is and how to switch off safely, and give them the paperwork. Finally I would meet with the team and supervisor to review the job: what went well, what went wrong, and what we would plan differently next time.
markingPoints: Leaves the work safe and complete
Cleans up and sorts waste correctly
Returns tools and materials and reports damage
Updates drawings and completes the job records
Hands over to the customer and reviews the job with the team

practical1.title: Prepare a complete work plan for a small wiring job
practical1.brief: The instructor gives the group a job card and drawing for a small job on a training bay: one lighting point with a switch, and one socket outlet, wired in conduit from the bay's practice panel. As a group, prepare a complete written work plan. It must include: the job requirements in your own words; a list of steps in order with a time for each; a bar chart; a materials list with quantities and a tools list; a risk assessment with controls, including safe isolation; the quality checks and dead tests you will do; and the clean-up and reporting steps. Share the work so that each member writes at least one section, then each member explains their section to the assessor. Photograph each document and the presentation and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group with all the documents.
materials: Job card and drawing from the instructor
Blank planning forms: step list, bar chart, materials and tools list, risk assessment, quality check sheet
Scale rule, tape measure, calculator, pens and pencils
The Centre's store price or stock list (if available)
Flip chart paper or a whiteboard for the presentation
photos: The job requirements written in the group's own words
The list of steps in order, with times
The materials list with quantities, and the tools list
The completed risk assessment, showing safe isolation
The quality check sheet and clean-up steps
Each member explaining their section to the assessor
checklist: Read the job card and drawing and wrote the requirements correctly
Put the steps in a sensible order with realistic times
Drew a bar chart that matches the step list
Worked out quantities from the drawing, with an allowance for waste
Listed hazards and controls, with safe isolation described correctly
Planned stage checks and the dead tests in the right order
Wrote at least one section and explained it clearly
Worked with the group and listened to others
safety: This task is done in the classroom; keep bags and cables off walkways
The plan must never include live work; isolation is always shown first
Follow the Centre's rules for the classroom and the training bays

practical2.title: Carry out a planned task on a training bay and review it
practical2.brief: As a group, carry out a short task on a training bay from a plan: mark out and fix PVC conduit, a switch box, a light box and a socket box to the drawing the instructor gives. No cables are connected and the bay is not connected to any supply. Before starting, hold a short toolbox talk on the tasks and hazards. Use the bar chart to check progress at set times, and write down any problem and how it was solved. When finished, check your work against the drawing, clean up and complete a short job report and a review sheet: what went well, what went wrong and what you would change next time. Every member fixes at least one section of conduit or one box, and every member writes one point on the review sheet. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: The plan and drawing from the instructor (or the group's own plan from Practical 1)
20 mm PVC conduit, couplers, saddles and boxes as listed in the plan
Hacksaw, conduit bending spring, file, tape measure, spirit level, pencil
Drill and fixings to suit the training bay
photos: The group at the toolbox talk, with the plan on show
The bay marked out to the drawing
Work in progress at the first progress check, with the bar chart marked up
The finished conduit and boxes, with a spirit level on the run
The problem log showing any change and how it was agreed
The bay and floor cleaned, and tools returned
The completed job report and review sheet
checklist: Took part in the toolbox talk and knew their tasks and the hazards
Marked out and fixed their section to the drawing, level and secure
Used hand and power tools safely, with PPE
Checked progress against the bar chart and reported any delay
Reported a problem to the assessor instead of changing the plan alone
Checked the finished work against the drawing
Cleaned up, sorted waste and returned tools
Wrote a sensible point on the review sheet
safety: The training bay is not connected to any supply during this task
Wear safety glasses when cutting conduit and drilling
Check the drill, cable and plug before use; report any damage
Keep tools, off-cuts and cables off the floor and walkways
Follow the Centre's rules for the training bays
